title: Democracies Are Falling Behind on Safe Drinking Water, MIT Study Finds
summary: Clean water is a basic human need, yet roughly 2 billion people — a quarter of the world's population — lack regular access to it. And about 800,000 die each year from diseases linked to unsanitary water. You might assume that democratic governments, with their elections and accountability, would lead the charge in solving this. But a surprising new study from MIT political scientist Evan Lieberman and Stanford doctoral student Naomi Tilles suggests otherwise. The researchers analyzed data from 96 low- and middle-income countries between 2000 and 2024, running 39,000 statistical regressions. They found that democracies are modestly better at providing "basic" water access — defined as an improved source within 30 minutes of collection. However, when it comes to "safe" water — available on premises, when needed, and free of contaminants like fecal matter or chemicals — democracies have been falling behind non-democracies. "For safe drinking water, we found, surprisingly, that democratic countries were becoming less good at extending access," Lieberman said. The gap is widening over time. Why? The researchers point to a visibility problem. Democracies excel at delivering visible public goods — things like pipes and taps that politicians can showcase at ribbon-cutting ceremonies. But water quality is invisible. Testing, treating, and preventing pollution don't make for good photo ops. "Politicians may figure out they should do things citizens like, to stay in office, such as bringing water to an area," Lieberman explained. "But water quality is often invisible. It's a more difficult challenge." The study doesn't pinpoint exact causes but suggests that incentives are misaligned. The good news: 81 of 90 countries with data in both years made gains in safe water access. Yet the democratic advantage is eroding. Lieberman, an expert on African politics and author of "Until We Have Won Our Liberty," still believes democracy offers "dignified development" with liberties and equal treatment. But for safe water, he says, "the incentives are not aligned under the current systems." The findings, published in World Development, call for new strategies to make safe water a political priority — because what you can't see can still hurt you.
why_it_matters: For teenagers who will soon become voters and taxpayers, this study exposes a hidden weakness in how democracies work — it shows that even well‑meaning governments can neglect problems you can’t easily see, making it important to learn how to hold elected officials accountable for invisible, life‑threatening issues like water quality.

background_read: In 2010, the United Nations officially recognized access to clean drinking water and sanitation as a human right, yet billions still go without. Political scientists have long debated whether democracy helps or hinders the delivery of basic services like water, roads, and electricity.

Evan Lieberman (an MIT professor and author of ‘Until We Have Won Our Liberty,’ a book about South Africa’s democracy) studies how governments in Africa meet citizens’ needs. The study’s co‑author, Naomi Tilles, is a doctoral candidate at Stanford University researching global development.

The visibility problem is not new: even in wealthy nations, tainted water often stays hidden until a crisis erupts. For example, in Flint, Michigan (a U.S. city), lead leached into drinking water for months before state officials acknowledged it, proving that quality can slip even in an established democracy.

Non‑democratic countries like China have sometimes built massive water infrastructure quickly, partly because leaders can direct resources without voter pressure. This study adds evidence that in democracies, politicians’ incentives may be mismatched with long‑term needs like water quality.
Article_Structure: LEAD: Startling statistic — 2 billion lack clean water, 800,000 die yearly from unsafe water.
KEY CLAIM: Democracies are assumed to be better at providing public goods, but the study overturns that for safe water.
METHOD: Researchers analyzed data from 96 low- and middle-income countries, running 39,000 regressions.
├─ DEFINITIONS: 'Basic' water (improved source within 30 min) vs 'safe' water (on premises, contaminant‑free).
FINDINGS: Democracies slightly better at basic water; but falling behind non‑democracies on safe water, gap widening.
EXPLANATION: The visibility problem — politicians prefer visible pipes and taps over invisible water quality.
└─ QUOTE: Lieberman says politicians respond to things voters can see; water quality is an invisible, difficult challenge.
GOOD NEWS / COMPLICATION: 81 out of 90 countries made gains, yet the democratic advantage is eroding.
AUTHOR'S STANCE: Lieberman still values democracy’s dignity, but incentives are not aligned for safe water.
OUTRO: Study in World Development calls for new strategies to make safe water a political priority.

perspectives.description: The study’s clear evidence gives reformers a target: align politicians’ incentives with safe water. Many countries still made progress, showing that even with flawed systems, improvements are possible. Democracies still offer freedoms that can empower activists to demand better monitoring.

The widening gap is alarming; democracies that pride themselves on government by the people are failing at the most fundamental service — safe drinking water. The invisible nature of quality means politicians can easily ignore it, leading to preventable deaths from diarrheal diseases that hit children hardest.

This fits a well‑studied pattern in political economy: democratic governments tend to supply what voters can see (pipes, roads, schools) while neglecting technical, long‑term goods. The study’s use of 39,000 regressions is a rigorous way to control for other factors, strengthening the case that the problem is systemic rather than an accident.

The findings could spark new policies such as mandatory public reporting of water quality tests, independent oversight agencies, or tying international aid to improvements in invisible public goods. Young people entering STEM, law, or political science could build these systems, turning data into action.
